newsitem.title: COMOROS: Bodies dangle upside down in Ethiopian plane wreck.
newsitem.headline: Bodies dangle upside down in Ethiopian plane wreck.

text.p: A section of the Ethiopian Airlines plane that crashed on Saturday off the Comoro Islands was winched upside down onto the beach on Monday with bodies dangling from the seats they were still strapped into.

The plane, hijacked en route to Nairobi and West Africa from Addis Ababa, ran out of fuel over the Indian Ocean archipelago and ditched into the sea, some 500 metres (yards) off a tourist beach on this idyllic Indian Ocean archipelago.
Fifty-two of the 175 passengers and crew survived, according to Ethiopian Airlines. The other 123 are dead or presumed dead. Around 40 bodies remained in the wreckage on Monday morning.

Comoros police workers hauled the mid-section of the plane's cabin onto the beach by moonlight with a truck and cable after they finally lost patience with French experts who wanted to wait for special salvage equipment to arrive from the French Reunion island.

Comoros police workers hauled the plane section onto the beach by moonlight with a truck and cable after they finally lost patience with French experts who wanted to wait for special salvage equipment to arrive from the French Reunion island.

"They came and said to wait for special material. I said that's not normal. You can't just leave all those bodies putrefying, near to the hotel," Captain Jimmy Ibrahim Ali, in charge of operations for the Comoran gendarmerie, told Reuters.
The mid-section of the cabin was now upside down on the beach, one wing-tip lying limply in the sand, another in the water.
Tourists, some of whom had rushed to help the survivors on Saturday, were now taking photos of the rescue effort, held back from the wreckage by a police cordon.
Rescue workers said they could see some bodies strapped into their seats, dangling down inside the wreck.
"We can see them, but they're belted in. We're getting a chainsaw to cut our way in," Ali said.

The Comoran police were using hacksaws and anything else that came to hand to break into the wreck. They pulled out one more body on Monday morning, that of a woman in shorts, still clutching a small, black rucksack.
Police said some bodies remained inside the front section of the plane which, with the cockpit, was under water and unlikely to be salvaged immediately.
The back of the plane was also still in the sea, the green bit of the green-red-and-yellow tail visible above the water.
The special cutting equipment from Reunion had still not arrived on Monday morning.
"We're very annoyed," Ali said. "We'll cope our own way."

However, Bruce Thomson, resident manager of Le Galawa hotel opposite the scene of the crash, said he had been told the French needed permission from the Comoran government to retrieve the bodies, and that might explain their hesitation.
Parts of the wrecked plane were being lined up on the beach for accident investigators to examine. U.S. forensic experts had also arrived at the Comoros.

Among the crash survivors was the Ethiopian pilot, Leul Abate, 42, who suffered head injuries. He had identified two of the suspected hijackers among the other survivors and they had been arrested by the police.
Ethiopia on Monday asked the government of the Comoros to extradite the two, both Ethiopian nationals.
The third hijacker died in the crash. Rumours on the Comoros that one of the detained suspects had also died could not be confirmed.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi thanked the Comorans for their "prompt and exceptional" rescue effort and said: "The Comoros would take appropriate and prompt action in handing over the perpetrators of this heinous crime to Ethiopia (for trial)."
The Ethiopian government has declared three days of mourning for the crash victims.
Top African television cameraman Mohamed Amin was among the passengers who died. Amin, 53, of Reuters Television, won acclaim for bringing Ethiopia's disastrous 1984 famine to the eyes of the world.
